overview.short_description: A mild, self-limiting viral infection of the upper respiratory tract causing nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea, sore throat and cough, resolving in about a week.
overview.detailed_description: The most common acute illness in humans. Caused by many respiratory viruses (rhinoviruses most often, also coronaviruses, RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, metapneumovirus). Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are unnecessary. The main clinical task is to distinguish it from conditions needing specific treatment (influenza, streptococcal pharyngitis, acute sinusitis, lower respiratory infection, COVID-19) and to reassure and give symptomatic advice, avoiding unnecessary antibiotics.
overview.pathophysiology: Viral infection of respiratory epithelium triggers an inflammatory response (cytokines, increased vascular permeability, mucus secretion) producing congestion, rhinorrhoea and sneezing. Symptoms are largely from the host inflammatory response rather than tissue destruction.
overview.etiology: Respiratory viruses transmitted by droplets, aerosols and contaminated surfaces (hand-to-mucosa). Rhinovirus is the leading cause.
overview.natural_history: Symptoms peak at days 2-3 and resolve within 7-10 days; cough may linger 2-3 weeks. Complications are uncommon.
overview.prognosis: Excellent — self-limiting. Complications (otitis media, sinusitis, lower respiratory infection, asthma exacerbation) are uncommon.

prevalence.value: Adults ~2-4 colds/year, children ~6-8/year (higher with nursery/school exposure).

incidence.value: Extremely high; the commonest reason for primary-care visits and time off work/school.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; young children most frequently affected.
epidemiology.seasonal_pattern: More common in autumn and winter in temperate climates.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Close contact/crowding, poor hand hygiene, inadequate sleep, psychological stress.
risk_factors.diabetes: Not a major factor; poor control may impair immunity slightly.
risk_factors.pregnancy: Not a risk factor, but decongestant choice is restricted in pregnancy.
risk_factors.occupation: Teachers, childcare, healthcare workers have higher exposure.
risk_factors.travel: Crowded travel (planes, public transport) increases exposure.
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Asthma/COPD — colds are a common trigger for exacerbations.

symptoms.importance: Core symptom; colour change alone does NOT indicate bacterial infection
High or prominent fever/myalgia should raise suspicion of influenza or COVID-19

negative_findings.finding: No high fever, rigors, or prominent myalgia
negative_findings.why_important: Their absence makes influenza less likely and supports simple cold

negative_findings.finding: No breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, or focal chest signs
negative_findings.why_important: Absence argues against pneumonia/lower respiratory infection

negative_findings.finding: No tonsillar exudate, tender cervical nodes, or absence of cough (Centor features)
negative_findings.why_important: Fewer Centor features makes streptococcal pharyngitis less likely

history_questions.question: How long have symptoms lasted and are they improving or worsening?
history_questions.why_ask: Colds improve by ~7-10 days; worsening after initial improvement suggests bacterial sinusitis

history_questions.question: Do you have high fever, severe muscle aches, or sudden onset?
history_questions.why_ask: Points to influenza rather than a cold

history_questions.question: Any breathlessness, chest pain, or coughing up blood?
Any relevant contacts, recent travel, or need for COVID-19 testing?
Do you have asthma/COPD or are you immunocompromised/pregnant?
history_questions.why_ask: Higher-risk groups need closer review and safe medication choices

physical_examination.expected_finding: Well or mildly unwell; low-grade or no fever

physical_examination.examination: ENT: nose (congested mucosa), throat (mild erythema, no exudate)
Cervical lymph nodes and ears (especially children)
physical_examination.expected_finding: Usually normal; check for otitis media in children

vital_signs.temperature: Normal or low-grade fever (high/persistent fever suggests another diagnosis)
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: Normal (>=95%); low saturation is a red flag

laboratory_tests.indication: Not needed for a typical cold
Public-health need, high-risk contacts, or uncertain diagnosis
laboratory_tests.diagnostic_value: Rarely changes management of a simple cold

imaging.when_needed: Consider chest X-ray only if lower respiratory infection suspected

other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Throat swab only if streptococcal pharyngitis suspected by score
other_diagnostic_tests.pcr: Respiratory viral / COVID-19 PCR only when result would change management or for public health

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical diagnosis: acute onset of coryzal symptoms (nasal congestion, rhinorrhoea, sneezing, sore throat, cough) without features pointing to a specific alternative (high fever/myalgia of influenza, Centor features of strep, persistent worsening course of sinusitis, or lower respiratory signs).
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: No score for the cold itself; Centor/McIsaac scores help exclude streptococcal pharyngitis.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Sudden onset, high fever, marked myalgia, prostration
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Was onset sudden with high fever and body aches?
Any loss of smell/taste or known contact?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender nodes, ABSENCE of cough
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Do you have a cough? (its presence argues against strep)

differential_diagnosis.differences: Symptoms >10 days or worsening after initial improvement, facial pain, purulent discharge
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Did you improve then get worse, with facial pain?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Itchy eyes/nose, no fever, seasonal/trigger pattern, chronic/recurrent
differential_diagnosis.distinguishing_symptoms: Itch, sneezing bouts, clear persistent rhinorrhoea
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Are your eyes/nose itchy and is it triggered by seasons/animals?

diagnostic_questions.question: Was the onset gradual (cold) or sudden with high fever and body aches (influenza)?
Do you have a cough along with the sore throat?

next_best_question.question: Are your symptoms improving, and do you have any breathlessness or high fever?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Improving/no red flags vs worsening/red flags
next_best_question.branching_logic: Improving, no red flags -> reassure + symptomatic advice; worsening/red flags -> examine for sinusitis/LRTI/influenza

next_best_test.why: A typical cold needs no test
Public health, high-risk contact, or diagnostic uncertainty

red_flags.finding: Breathlessness, rapid breathing, or oxygen saturation <95%
High persistent fever, marked lethargy, or looking seriously unwell
Neck stiffness, photophobia, non-blanching rash, or severe headache
Symptoms worsening after 10 days or 'double-sickening' with facial pain
In infants: poor feeding, reduced wet nappies, grunting, chest recession

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Suspected pneumonia in a high-risk patient not manageable in the community; suspected serious bacterial complication.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Recurrent/persistent symptoms suggesting an alternative diagnosis (e.g., chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy).
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Respiratory distress/hypoxia, suspected meningitis/sepsis, or a seriously unwell infant.

initial_management.supportive_care: Reassurance that it is self-limiting; rest and adequate fluids; explain expected course and safety-net advice.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; Decongestant. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: CDC_COLD_2026.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Hydration, rest, hand hygiene to reduce spread; avoid smoking.
initial_management.follow_up: No routine follow-up; return if symptoms persist beyond ~10 days, worsen, or red flags develop.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Symptomatic only: paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever/aches; saline nasal drops/spray; short-term topical or oral decongestants for congestion (avoid prolonged topical use; caution in hypertension/pregnancy); honey (>1 year old) for cough. ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT INDICATED for an uncomplicated viral cold.

patient_education.home_advice: A cold is caused by a virus and gets better on its own in about a week; antibiotics do not help. Rest, drink fluids, and use paracetamol or ibuprofen for aches and fever. Wash your hands to avoid spreading it. See a doctor if you become breathless, have a high fever that won't settle, cough up blood, or don't improve after about 10 days.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: نزلة البرد سببها فيروس وتتحسّن وحدها خلال أسبوع تقريباً، والمضادات الحيوية لا تفيدها. ارتَح واشرب السوائل واستخدم الباراسيتامول أو الإيبوبروفين للألم والحرارة، واغسل يديك لتجنّب نقل العدوى. راجع الطبيب إذا صرت تلهث، أو استمرّت حرارة عالية، أو خرج دم مع السعال، أو لم تتحسّن بعد نحو 10 أيام.
patient_education.prevention: Regular hand washing, avoiding close contact with unwell people, not touching the face; there is no vaccine for the common cold.
patient_education.warning_signs: Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, high unremitting fever, confusion, neck stiffness, or no improvement after 10 days.

prevention.vaccination: No vaccine for the common cold (influenza and COVID-19 vaccines target those specific viruses, not colds).
prevention.lifestyle: Hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, adequate sleep, not smoking.

evidence.evidence_level: High for the self-limiting nature and lack of antibiotic benefit; moderate for symptomatic remedies.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by CDC_COLD_2026; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong — NICE CKS, AAFP; antibiotic avoidance strongly recommended.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Support recovery and avoid ineffective antibiotics or unsafe OTC combinations.

Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Paracetamol; NSAID; Decongestant. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: CDC_COLD_2026.

pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances

non_drug_measures: Rest, fluids, saline and honey only for people older than 1 year; antibiotics do not treat uncomplicated viral cold.
